name: New England Federal

revival_periods.note: New England Federal is the single largest donor to the Colonial Revival image bank: the fanlighted door, the Palladian window over it, and the balustraded hip roof.

lineage.note: Direct craft continuity. The same housewrights, the same white pine clapboard over braced frame, the same central-chimney-derived plan discipline; only the mouldings changed.
Bulfinch saw Adam's work in England in 1785-87 and carried it back as first-hand observation rather than as printed plates - the one American case where the Adam transmission is direct.

description.short: The Federal style executed in white-painted clapboard and Charlestown brick by the housewrights of Boston, Salem and the Maine coast, at its best a wooden architecture pretending, very thinly, to be a masonry one.
description.long:
New England Federal is what happens when a masonry style is handed to a carpentry culture with the best softwood in the Atlantic world and a shortage of both stone and plasterers. The urban version - Bulfinch's Boston, the brick fronts of Beacon Hill and Salem's Chestnut Street - is genuinely Adamesque: three-storey brick with graduated storey heights, a marble stringcourse, a fanlighted door, and a hipped roof behind a balustrade. The rural and coastal version is the more interesting one, because there everything Adam did in stucco and stone is being executed in clear white pine with moulding planes. Fluted pilasters at the corners are boards. The 'quoins' are cut into a board. The elliptical fanlight is joinery. The whole facade is painted white so that at a distance it does not read as wood at all, which is exactly the intention: this is a carpenter's imitation of a mason's architecture, performed so competently that the imitation became the regional idiom.

The conditions were maritime and brief. Between the Peace of Paris and the Embargo of 1807, the New England carrying trade made a class of merchants in Boston, Salem, Newburyport, Portsmouth, Providence and the Maine ports rich very quickly, and they built. Salem's Chestnut Street and Portsmouth's Middle Street are the physical residue of the East Indies and the neutral-carrying trade. Samuel McIntire in Salem, Charles Bulfinch in Boston, Asher Benjamin as the publishing intermediary, and dozens of housewrights working from Benjamin's plates supplied the design. Timber supply mattered as much as taste: eastern white pine in wide clear widths, easily worked and dimensionally stable, made possible the very thin muntins and crisp shallow mouldings that define the style, and made it cheap to imitate stone forms in wood. When the trade collapsed after 1807 and again after 1812, so did the building, and the coast is full of superb Federal houses that were essentially the last thing their towns could afford - Wiscasset and Columbia Falls, Maine, are museums of this fact.

What it reacts against, within New England, is the massive central chimney and the steep dark roof of the colonial house. The Federal generation moved the chimneys to the gable ends or into paired interior stacks, dropped the pitch, opened the plan around a stair hall, and doubled the glass area. The result is a demonstrably brighter, colder, more expensive house - a deliberate trade of thermal sense for light and formality, made by people who could now afford to heat four fireplaces instead of hoarding one. The three-storey brick townhouse version goes further still and abandons the free-standing house entirely for the party wall, which in Boston produced the finest American urbanism before 1850.

Inside a good one the effect is of thinness and light. Rooms are eleven or twelve feet high on the principal floor with windows nearly to the ceiling, and the woodwork is all edge: reeded pilasters an inch and a half wide, a mantel of applied composition swags, a chair rail that is a band rather than a moulding. McIntire's carving in Salem is so shallow you have to stand at an angle to see it. The stair, where the money went, curves out of the hall and rises without any visible means of support - the Ruggles House in Columbia Falls has one built by a housewright in a town of a few hundred people, and standing under it is the closest American domestic architecture gets to a magic trick.

defining_characteristics: Federal proportions and Adamesque detail executed predominantly in painted white pine over a braced timber frame, or in brick in the seaport cities
Gable-end or paired interior chimneys replacing the colonial central stack, with a low hip or side-gable roof
Roof frequently hipped and screened by a balustrade or captain's walk; pitch dropped well below colonial practice
Elliptical fanlight and sidelight entrance, often with a small semicircular or elliptical portico on slender colonnettes
Palladian or triple window centred over the entrance on the principal facade
Corner treatment by flat fluted pilasters or applied wood 'quoins' - masonry gestures executed in board
Wide, thin, crisply run mouldings possible only in clear eastern white pine
diagnostic_tells: Wood imitating masonry: flat pilasters at the corners, rusticated or quoined boards, all painted white
A semicircular or elliptical entrance portico so small and slender it shelters nothing - it is a frame, not a roof
Palladian window stacked directly over the fanlight door, a New England signature the South used far less
Balustrade or captain's walk on a low hip roof, in a region whose colonial houses had steep gables and a huge central chimney
Four-chimney silhouette (paired interior stacks) rather than one massive central stack

distinguished_from.difference: Same frame, same clapboard, same town. The Georgian house has a central chimney or heavy paired stacks, a steeper roof, a projecting pedimented door frontispiece, and muntins over an inch. The Federal house has a lower hip, thin muntins, a fanlight set flush in the wall, and graduated storey heights.

New England builds tight, tall and closed - three storeys, low hip, no porch, windows shut against the winter. Southern Federal builds wide and one room deep with piazzas, taller ground-floor ceilings, and often a raised basement. The plan responds to opposite climates within an identical ornamental vocabulary.

Revival work enlarges the fanlight assembly, thickens muntins, and combines Federal doorways with gambrel roofs, sunrooms and attached garages. Genuine New England Federal doorways are smaller than photographs suggest and sit on a house whose upper windows are visibly shorter than its lower ones.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Adamesque classical proportion transmitted through Bulfinch's first-hand observation and Asher Benjamin's plates, executed to the tolerances of hand-run wood mouldings rather than plaster.
typical_ratios: Three-storey brick townhouse: storey heights approximately 12 : 10 : 7.5 feet
Two-and-a-half-storey frame house: 9.5-11 feet ground floor, second floor 0.85-0.9 of it
Colonnette height 10-11 diameters on entrance porticoes
Clapboard exposure 4-5 inches on principal facades, 5-6 inches on secondary elevations
Roof pitch 6:12 to 8:12 hipped, against 9:12-12:12 in the colonial work it replaced
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Five-bay frame houses and three-bay townhouses with even spacing; the Palladian window over the door is the only permitted disturbance of the rhythm and it must be centred.

massing_affinities.note: Beacon Hill, Salem's Chestnut Street, Providence's Benefit Street.
Gore Place is the outstanding New England case and is rare precisely because the region's wealth was mercantile and urban rather than agricultural.

constraints.statement: Where masonry forms are executed in wood (pilasters, quoins, rustication), the board thickness must not exceed 1-1/4 inch and the whole assembly must be painted a single light colour. Exposed wood grain or contrasting trim colour destroys the masonry illusion the variant depends on.
Sash 6/6 or 6/9 with muntins 5/8 to 7/8 inch; glass 10 x 14 to 12 x 18 inches. Upper-storey window height must be 0.80-0.90 of the principal storey, and third-storey 0.60-0.75.

test.note: Tests the upper-storey-to-principal-storey window/storey height diminishing pair (10-20 percent, ratio 0.80-0.90). Sash light pattern, muntin width (5/8-7/8in), glass size (10x14-12x18in) and the third-storey diminishing ratio (0.60-0.75) are left as prose.

constraints.statement: Central chimney is forbidden. Chimneys must be at the gable ends or paired as interior stacks flanking the stair hall - the plan liberation that distinguishes the variant from its colonial parent.

test.note: Tests that chimney_position excludes interior-central, capturing 'central chimney is forbidden'. paired-exterior is the closest available vocabulary match for 'paired as interior stacks flanking the stair hall' -- the enum has no paired-interior value -- so this is a flagged approximation, not an exact test of the interior-stack claim.

constraints.statement: Roof pitch 6:12 to 8:12 (hip or low side gable) - low enough to read Federal, steep enough to shed New England snow. Below 5:12 the assembly fails in zone 5A-6A snow loads and above 9:12 it reads colonial.
Entrance portico, where present, is limited to a single storey and a projection of 4-6 feet on colonnettes no more than 7 inches in diameter. It is a frame for the door, not a shelter.

test.note: Tests the portico projection depth (4-6ft) via balcony_depth_ft, reused for a comparable cantilevered/posted projection -- flagged as an approximation since the vocabulary entry's canonical case is a balcony, not a portico. The single-storey limit and the 7in colonnette-diameter cap are left as prose -- no column-diameter vocabulary variable exists.

exemplars.name: First Harrison Gray Otis House
exemplars.note: Charles Bulfinch; brick, three storeys, five bays, Palladian window above the entrance with a lunette above that.
exemplars.why: Bulfinch, and the single building the Boston brick Federal is known by; the HABS inventory sheet states its five bays and three storeys in those words, and the federal-style node already reads it the same way.

exemplars.name: Gore Place
exemplars.note: Five-part brick country house about 190 feet long with bowed oval projections; plans developed with the French architect Jacques-Guillaume Legrand.
exemplars.why: The five-part country house, documented and open, and the National Historic Landmark statement quoted on its HABS sheet calls it 'a noteworthy example of a five-part Federal house'.

exemplars.name: Nickels-Sortwell House
exemplars.location: Main and Federal Streets, Wiscasset, Maine
exemplars.note: Built 1807-08 for shipmaster William Nickels; the fullest expression of the coastal Maine merchant Federal, with a monumental two-storey entrance frontispiece in wood.
exemplars.why: The coastal Maine merchant Federal at full stretch, and the Maine Historic Preservation Commission ties its doorway to Plate 20 of Asher Benjamin's 1806 American Builder's Companion -- one of this node's own four sources, named on the building.

exemplars.name: Ruggles House
exemplars.note: Built 1818-20 by housewright Aaron Sherman with carving by Alvah Peterson; the free-flying stair rises to a landing and reverses without visible support in a village of a few hundred people.
exemplars.why: The Down East village Federal at the end of the carrying trade, and 'outstanding because of its craftsmanship rather than for its beauty of design' is the 1937 surveyor's own verdict on it.

exemplars.name: Gardner-Pingree House
exemplars.note: Samuel McIntire for John Gardner. The brick Salem front, and the other half of this node's hearth: Bulfinch's Otis House is the Boston case and this is the Salem one. HABS recorded it as the Gardner-White-Pingree Place (MA-271) and the extractor has so far returned only the survey's cover, so no figure of its own is on the record yet.
exemplars.why: This node names two hearths, Boston and Salem, and one icon can only stand for one of them; this is the Salem one, and the attribution to McIntire is the standard reading the federal-style node already carries.

exemplars.name: Rundlet-May House
exemplars.note: Portsmouth's three-storey merchant Federal: five bays under a low hip with a wooden balustrade, four chimneys paired at the ends, clapboard rather than brick. James Rundlet's building ledger survives and puts the cost at $12,604.47, more than half of it labour and board, with as many as eighteen men on site.
exemplars.why: There is no HABS survey and it is carried for the ledger instead: the house's own interpretive site, reading the surviving ledger labelled 'Building House 1806-1809', calls it 'perhaps one of the best documented houses in terms of knowing how the laborers worked, what materials they used and how much the materials cost; right down to the cost of nails', and a construction account is worth more to this node than another photograph.

sources: Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Asher Benjamin, The American Builder's Companion (1806)
Abbott Lowell Cummings, The Framed Houses of Massachusetts Bay, 1625-1725 (1979), for the framing tradition this variant inherits
William H. Pierson Jr., American Buildings and Their Architects: The Colonial and Neoclassical Styles (1970)
Historic New England property files (Otis House, Nickels-Sortwell House)

proportion_packs.note: The one order run throughout this variant rather than a graded primary/secondary pair -- unlike georgian-colonial-american's Ionic-for-best-rooms/Doric-for-everyday-work hierarchy, Federal ornament is uniformly thin, and this style's own defining_characteristics name the SAME order for both the corner pilasters and the entrance: 'fluted pilasters at the corners' and, in its own typical_ratios, 'colonnette height 10-11 diameters on entrance porticoes.' This pack's column is 20 semidiameter-modules, i.e. exactly 10 diameters -- the bottom of that stated range on the nose. Benjamin over Gibbs because Bulfinch (who designed this variant's own leading exemplar, the Otis House) saw Adam's work in England first-hand in 1785-87 and Benjamin's 1816 plates are the documented transmission for everyone who came after him.

The wall_section_federal / casing_federal family. McIntire's Salem carving is 'so shallow you have to stand at an angle to see it' per the style's own description -- the flattest possible expression of the family this pack encodes, executed here in clear eastern white pine rather than plaster, which is what let the mouldings run this thin and crisp in the first place.

Ranked ahead of opening-proportion, matching the parent style: constraint c02 states the muntin ceiling directly (5/8-7/8 in) and glass size (10x14 to 12x18 in), and the pack's own rule that it wins any disagreement with opening-proportion on window ratio is the reason for the ordering.

Governs door and window sizing beneath the fanlight-and-sidelight co-occurrence rule the parent style states (single-storey entrance treatment only; a two-storey portico is forbidden). This variant's own description notes the entrance portico 'shelters nothing -- it is a frame, not a roof,' which constraint c05 makes explicit: single storey, 4-6 ft projection, colonnettes no more than 7 in diameter.

Governs the elevation composition -- five-bay frame houses, three-bay townhouses, the centred Palladian window as the only tolerated disturbance of the bay rhythm -- through the same reduced-projection ceiling federal-style's own binding of this pack states (3 in general, 6 in at the door surround).

This variant states its own three-storey townhouse ratio directly -- storey heights approximately 12 : 10 : 7.5 ft -- which is close to but slightly steeper than this pack's default compounding (0.85 then 0.80, i.e. 12 / 10.2 / 8.16 on a 12 ft base); the variant's own figure is bound as the governing case and the pack supplies the general mechanism and the window-follows-the-storey rule that makes the diminution legible from the street.

Listed directly in this pack's applies_to cross-reference. Bound for the oval and circular rooms this variant's own description names as its interior signature -- Gore Place's bowed oval projections, the free-flying stair at the Ruggles House -- composed geometry rather than accumulated framing.

PROMOTED ABOVE brick-course here, the reverse of southern-federal's ordering. This variant's own description states plainly that 'the rural and coastal version is the more interesting one' and that the whole enterprise is 'a carpenter's imitation of a mason's architecture' -- clear white pine over a braced frame is the characteristic fabric, with the Boston/Salem brick townhouse as the secondary, urban case.
The seaport brick minority -- Beacon Hill, Salem's Chestnut Street -- bound optional and demoted below timber-bay for this variant specifically, the inverse of the ranking on southern-federal.
